title: Family, and how to describe people
goal: Talk about your family — which in Indonesia is the first thing anyone will ask you about — and put adjectives where Indonesian wants them: after the noun, never before.
bekal: answer the standard Indonesian interview: married? children? how many brothers and sisters?
describe a person or a thing with the adjective in the right place

dialogs.title: Dialogue — Pertanyaan wajib
dialogs.intro: In the office pantry. Bu Wati, a colleague in her fifties, has decided it is time to get to know the newcomer.

lines.speaker: Wati:
lines.id: Oh, still young. How many are you in the family?

lines.speaker: Sarah:
lines.id: There are three of us. I'm the second child.

lines.speaker: Wati:
lines.id: Is your older sibling a brother or a sister?

lines.speaker: Sarah:
lines.text: Kakak saya laki-laki. Adik saya perempuan.
lines.id: My older sibling is a brother. My younger one is a sister.
lines.literal: older-sibling I male. younger-sibling I female.

lines.speaker: Wati:
lines.id: Do your parents live in Australia?

lines.speaker: Sarah:
lines.text: Ya. Ayah saya guru, ibu saya dokter.
lines.id: Yes. My father is a teacher and my mother is a doctor.
lines.literal: yes. father I teacher, mother I doctor.

lines.speaker: Wati:
lines.id: Wonderful! Is this a family photo?

lines.speaker: Sarah:
lines.text: Ya. Yang tinggi itu kakak saya.
lines.id: Yes. The tall one is my brother.
lines.literal: yes. that-which tall that older-sibling I.

lines.speaker: Wati:
lines.id: Handsome! Does he have a girlfriend?

notes: **These questions are not intrusive in Indonesia; they are friendliness.** Are you married, how many children, how old are you, what is your religion, how much do you earn — all of these can arrive within ten minutes of meeting someone, from a colleague or a taxi driver. Nobody is prying; they are placing you in a social map. Answer as briefly as you like, and *belum* is always a graceful reply.

**Belum, not tidak, about marriage.** Answering *tidak menikah* sounds like a declaration of principle. *Belum* — "not yet" — is the expected, easy answer even from someone who has no intention of ever marrying.

**Kakak and adik, not brother and sister.** Indonesian splits siblings by age, not by sex: *kakak* is any older sibling, *adik* any younger one. If sex matters you add it: *kakak laki-laki* (older brother), *adik perempuan* (younger sister). English speakers find this genuinely hard to remember at first.
**Berapa bersaudara? counts everyone including you.** *Tiga bersaudara* means three children in total, not three siblings plus Sarah. Answer with the total.

**Yang tinggi itu — "the tall one".** *Yang* turns a description into a thing: *yang tinggi* = "the one who is tall", *yang merah* = "the red one", *yang murah* = "the cheap one". It is the single most useful small word in the language after *ada*, and it comes back in every unit from here on.

grammars.title: Adjectives go after the noun
body: Same rule you have already met twice: the noun first, then whatever describes it.
after: Look at the last two lines carefully, because they are the whole difficulty. *Rumah besar* is a phrase ("a big house"); *Rumah itu besar* is a sentence ("that house is big"). Nothing but word order tells them apart, and there is no verb to help you.
When several words pile up, the order is: noun → adjective → this/that → owner. *Mobil merah itu* (that red car), *rumah besar saya* (my big house).

grammars.title: The family
body: Indonesian family words are used constantly as forms of address, not just as labels.
after: *Om* and *tante* come from Dutch, and they are what children call any friendly adult. A foreign man in Indonesia will be called *om* by small children within a week of arriving.
⚠️ *Orang tua* means "parents" (literally "old people") and also, in another context, "an elderly person". *Orang tua saya* is always "my parents".

blocks.text: Indonesian adjectives are also verbs, in the sense that they need no "to be": *Dia tinggi* is a complete sentence.

To intensify, put *sekali* **after** the adjective or *sangat* **before** it: *besar sekali* and *sangat besar* both mean "very big". 💬 In conversation everyone says *banget*, and it goes after: *besar banget*.
⚠️ *Lama* is a trap. Of an object it means "old" (*mobil lama*, an old car); of time it means "a long while" (*sudah lama*, "for a long time now"). For an old **person** you need *tua*, never *lama*.
*Yang* takes any description and turns it into something you can point at, ask for or buy. It is how you say "the red one" without repeating the noun.

blocks.text: *Yang* is also how Indonesian builds "who" and "which" clauses: *orang yang tinggal di sini* — "the person who lives here". You will not need to build long ones at A1, but you will hear them constantly, and now you know where the sentence hinges.
